# Import the data
```{r}
# Import the longtable with all results
lt <- read.csv(file="../data/quant_longtable.csv")
lt$Programming_Seniority <- as.factor(lt$Programming_Seniority)
lt$Comment_Type[lt$Comment_Type=="None"] <- "0None"
lt$Participant.Correct <- lt$Correct_Passfail
lt$Perceived.Capture <- lt$Capture
lt$HasComment <- ifelse(lt$Comment_Type == "None", "NoComment", "Comment")
lt$HasComment <- factor(lt$HasComment, ordered=FALSE)
lt$Capture <- factor(lt$Capture, ordered = TRUE)         # Likert: 1 < 2 < 3 < ...
lt$Programming_Seniority <- factor(lt$Programming_Seniority, ordered=TRUE)
lt$LLM_Use <- factor(lt$LLM_Use, ordered=TRUE)
lt$Comment_Type <- factor(lt$Comment_Type, ordered=FALSE)
lt$Python_Knowledge <- factor(lt$Python_Knowledge, ordered=TRUE)
lt$Python_Use <- factor(lt$Python_Use, ordered=TRUE)
lt$Assertion_Experience <- factor(lt$Assertion_Experience, ordered=TRUE)
lt_Correct = lt[lt$Postcondition_Correct == "1",]
lt_Incorrect = lt[lt$Postcondition_Correct == "0",]
lt_None = lt[lt$Comment_Type=="None",]
lt_Exact = lt[lt$Comment_Type=="Exact",]
lt_Overspecified = lt[lt$Comment_Type=="Overspecified",]
lt_Underspecified = lt[lt$Comment_Type=="Underspecified",]
lt_Incorrect = lt[lt$Comment_Type=="Incorrect",]
```

  "4" = "Moderate",
  "5" = "A lot"
)

# Modified function with label mapping
summarize_and_plot <- function(data, var_name, plot_title, fill_color = "steelblue", label_map = NULL,  filename = NULL) {
  # Create summary
  summary_df <- data %>%
    count(.data[[var_name]]) %>%
    mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
  
  # Print summary
  cat(paste0(plot_title, " Summary:\n"))
  print(summary_df)
  cat("\n")
  
  # Create plot
  p <- ggplot(summary_df, aes(x = factor(.data[[var_name]]), y = n)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = fill_color) +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n, " (", round(prop*100, 1), "%)")), 
              vjust = -0.5, size = 7) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.10))) + 
    labs(title = "",
         x = plot_title,
         y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 18),  # x-axis labels
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 18),                          # y-axis labels
      axis.title.x = element_text(size = 18,),          # x-axis title
      axis.title.y = element_blank(),          # y-axis title
    )
  
  # Apply label mapping if provided
  if (!is.null(label_map)) {
    p <- p + scale_x_discrete(labels = label_map)
  }
  
  print(p)
  
  
  return(summary_df)
}

# Use the function with label mappings

# Postcondition Correctness

A Chisq test shows a significant difference ($\chi^2=46.018$, p<0.001) 
in participant 
tendency to accurately identify a correct postcondition versus participant 
tendency to accurately identify an incorrect postcondition. In the case of 
correct postconditions, 73.9\% of participant responses accurately identified 
them as correct. In the case of incorrect postconditions, however, only 
49.0\% of participant responses accurately identified them as incorrect. 
Furthermore, neither the correctness of the postcondition nor the accuracy of
the participant response significantly impacted participant confidence (p > 
0.1), which was high in all cases (Between 3.98 and 4.14 on a likert scale 
between 0 and 5). The figure below shows participant confidence 
distributions in four cases; the cases where the participant succeeds and 
fails to identify a correct postcondition, and the cases where the 
participant succeeds and fails to identify an incorrect postcondition. 
```{r}
mean(lt$Participant_Correct)
chisq.test(lt$Participant_Correct, lt$Postcondition_Correct)
# odds ratio
fisher.test(lt$Participant_Correct, lt$Postcondition_Correct)
aggregate(Participant_Correct ~ Postcondition_Correct, data = lt, FUN = mean)
model1 <- lmer(Accuracy_Confidence ~ Participant_Correct * Postcondition_Correct + (1 | Pid) + (1 | Function_Seen), 
              data = lt)
Anova(model1, type=2)
emmeans(model1, ~ Participant_Correct * Postcondition_Correct)
```

# Timing 

A linear model with participant accuracy and postcondition correctness as 
predictors and response time as the dependent variable shows a significant 
effect of participant accuracy on response time (p = 0.014), driven by the 
interaction effect between participant accuracy and postcondition correctness
(p = 0.002). When the postcondition is correct, participants take about 
the same amount of time to respond whether they are accurate or not (103.4 vs.
108.4 seconds on average). However, when the postcondition is incorrect, there
is a much larger difference; participants take an average of 123.0 seconds to 
successfuly identify an incorrect postcondition, versus an average of 97.1 
seconds when they fail to identify the postcondition as incorrect.
```{r}
model1 <- lmer(
  log(Time_To_Complete) ~ Participant_Correct * Postcondition_Correct + (1 | Pid) + (1 | Function_Seen),
  data   = lt,
)

Anova(model1, type=2)
emmeans(model1, ~ Participant_Correct * Postcondition_Correct, type = "response")


lt$predicted <- predict(model1)   # Save the predicted values
lt$residuals <- residuals(model1) # Save the residual values
# Keep originals as 0/1 for stats, make display version just for plotting
lt$interaction_group <- interaction(
  factor(lt$Participant_Correct,   levels = c(0,1), labels = c("Part: Wrong", "Part: Correct")),
  factor(lt$Postcondition_Correct, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("Post: Wrong", "Post: Correct")),
  sep = " & "
)

ggplot(lt, aes(x = interaction_group, y = log(Time_To_Complete))) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "lightgrey") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = interaction_group, yend = predicted), alpha = .2) +
  geom_point(aes(color = abs(residuals), size = abs(residuals))) +
  scale_color_continuous(low = "green", high = "red") +
  guides(color = "none", size = "none") +
  geom_point(aes(y = predicted), shape = 1) +
  theme_bw()

# 2. Check distribution of residuals directly
hist(residuals(model1), breaks = 30)

# 3. Or density plot
plot(density(residuals(model1)))
```

# Complexity

In the full nl2postcond corpus from which our stimuli were drawn, incorrect
postconditions are more complex than correct ones:
cyclomatic complexity (means 2.69 vs 2.18), cognitive complexity, Halstead
difficulty and the Shevrin and Maoz reading-complexity score (all Wilcoxon
rank-sum p < 0.001, Cliff's delta 0.19 to 0.25). This is a property of
LLM-generated postconditions, not of our stimulus set: whether our 26
correct/incorrect pairs are balanced on complexity, and whether complexity
explains the accuracy effect, is analysed at the postcondition level in
dataset_contextualization/Postcondition_Balance.Rmd (it is balanced, and it
does not).
```{r}
pool <- read.csv("../data/postcondition_corpora.csv") %>%
  filter(dataset == "nl2postcond_py", ablation == "SimplePromptNoRef")
pool$correct <- as.logical(toupper(pool$correct))  

table(pool$correct)
aggregate(cbind(Cyclomatic, Cognitive, Halstead_Difficulty, SM_Score) ~ correct, 
          data = pool, FUN = mean)

wilcox.test(Cyclomatic ~ correct, data = pool)
wilcox.test(Cognitive ~ correct, data = pool)
wilcox.test(Halstead_Difficulty ~ correct, data = pool)
wilcox.test(SM_Score ~ correct, data = pool)

```

# Completeness

We only have a completeness ground truth for correct postconditions; these 
values were derived in previous work~\cite{Endres24} by testing the percent 
of mutations captured by the assert statement. 
A Spearman correlation test shows a significant correlation (p < 0.001) 
between the ground-truth completeness percentage and participants' 
assessment of postcondition completeness, with a Spearman's rho value of 
0.18. Additionally, a Wilcoxon rank sum test shows that participants gave 
significantly (p < 0.001) higher completeness scores to correct 
postconditions than to incorrect ones (means = 2.66 vs 2.35).
This may indicate that participants could intuit 
the worse quality of incorrect postconditions even when they did not identify
them as incorrect.
```{r}
cor.test(lt_Correct$Actual.Capture, lt_Correct$Perceived.Capture)

wilcox.test(Perceived.Capture ~ Postcondition_Correct, data = lt)
aggregate(Perceived.Capture ~ Postcondition_Correct, data = lt, FUN = mean)

```

# Taxonomy 

We applied the proposed postcondition taxonomy from prior work~\cite{Endres24}
to investigate whether particular taxonomized patterns were more or less 
associated with participant correctness. 
For each construction pattern, we compared accuracy on postconditions that 
contained it versus accuracy on those that did not. Assertions with arithmetic 
equalities ($+14.7$ percentage points, 14/52 postconditions) and 
type checks ($+10.5$ pp, 8/52) had the largest advantages. Assertions with 
element-property checks ($-11.4$ pp, 8/52) and implications ($-9.6$ pp, 37/52) 
had the largest disadvantages.
```{r warning=FALSE}
patterns <- c("Type_Check", "Format_Check", "Arithmetic_Bounds", "Arithmetic_Equality", "Container_Property",
              "Element_Property", "Forall_Element_Property", "Implication", "Null_Check")
postconditions <- unique(lt[, c("Postcondition_Seen", patterns)])
taxonomy <- data.frame(
  pattern = patterns,
  postconditions = colSums(postconditions[, patterns]),
  accuracy_with = sapply(patterns, function(p) mean(lt$Participant_Correct[lt[[p]] == 1])),
  accuracy_without = sapply(patterns, function(p) mean(lt$Participant_Correct[lt[[p]] == 0])),
  accuracy_diff = sapply(patterns, function(p) mean(lt$Participant_Correct[lt[[p]] == 1])) - sapply(patterns, function(p) mean(lt$Participant_Correct[lt[[p]] == 0]))
)
taxonomy[order(-taxonomy$accuracy_with), ]

```

# Comment Types

We fit a general linear mixed effects model with participant accuracy as 
the dependent variable, postcondition correctness and comment type as 
fixed effects, and individual variability as a random effect. We found 
that the existance and type of comments did not significantly affect 
participant accuracy, and this was unaffected by postcondition correctness.
```{r}
model <- glmer(
  Participant_Correct ~ Comment_Type * Postcondition_Correct + (1 | Pid) + (1 | Function_Seen),
  family = binomial,
  data = lt,
)

summary(model)

Anova(model)

# Get odds ratios from fixed effects
exp(fixef(model))

# Or with confidence intervals
exp(confint(model, method = "Wald", parm = "beta_"))
```

# Comment Types Continued

However, when comparing to the existence of exact comments, we find that 
participants were significantly less accurate when comments were 
underspecified than when comments were exact (p = 0.037, OR = 0.58).
Anecdotally, participants were less likely to accurately identify a 
postcondition as correct or incorrect when the comment was underspecified
than when there was no comment at all.
This may indicate that given the existence of comments, the quality of 
the comment impacts whether it helps or hurts viewer understanding.
```{r}
exact_under <- lt

exact_under$Comment_Type <- as.character(exact_under$Comment_Type)
exact_under$Comment_Type[exact_under$Comment_Type == "0None"] <- "None"
exact_under$Comment_Type <- factor(exact_under$Comment_Type)

# Refit model
model_exact_under_1 <- glmer(
  Participant_Correct ~ Comment_Type + Postcondition_Correct + (1 | Pid) + (1|Function_Seen),
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data   = exact_under
)

summary(model_exact_under_1)
exp(fixef(model_exact_under_1))
```

# Comments x Confidence 

We found that underspecified comments were the only comment type where 
participants reported a significant difference in their confidence 
(p = 0.0053, emmeans = 3.99, 4.07, 4.10, 4.06, 4.25 for no comment, 
exact comments, incorect comments, overspecified comments, and 
underspecified comments, respectively). We did not find significant 
differences between reported confidence values when participants were 
correct versus when they were incorrect. This may indicate that confidence
does not always correlate with understanding, and that poor quality 
comments may unduly raise perceived understanding.
```{r}
library(lme4)

m_base <- lmer(
  Accuracy_Confidence ~ Comment_Type + (1 | Pid) + (1 | Function_Seen),
  data   = lt
)

summary(m_base)

emmeans(m_base, ~ Comment_Type)
```

# Comment types vs Timing

We fit a linear mixed effects model with log of participant response time as 
the predicted variable, comment type as a fixed effect, and individual 
difference and stimulus as random effects, and saw that comment type had a 
significant impact (p=0.022) on participant response time. Participants took 
the longest times to respond when looking at exact comments, and the shortest 
times to respond when there was no comment at all (emmeans = 94.3, 114.5, 105.3, 
109.6, 111.8 for no comment, exact comment, incorrect comment, overspecified
comment, and underspecified comment, respectively.)

```{r}
mean(lt$Time_To_Complete)
```

```{r}
library(lme4)

m_base <- lmer(
  log(Time_To_Complete) ~ Comment_Type + (1 | Pid) + (1 | Function_Seen),
  data   = lt
)

summary(m_base)

anova(m_base)

emmeans(m_base, ~ Comment_Type, type = "response" )

```

# Demographics 

We did not find that any of programming seniority, assertion experience, 
python knowledge, python use frequency, or llm use frequency significantly 
predicted a participant's tendency to accurately respond to questions about 
postcondition correctness. This may indicate that programmers of all 
experience levels would benefit from assistance with parsing postconditions.
```{r}
lt_filter_prog_sen = lt[lt$Programming_Seniority<5,]
model <- glm(
  Participant_Correct ~ Programming_Seniority + Assertion_Experience + 
    Python_Use + Python_Knowledge + LLM_Use,
  data = lt_filter_prog_sen,
  family = binomial
)

Anova(model)

model <- glm(
  Participant_Correct ~ Programming_Seniority,
  data = lt_filter_prog_sen,
  family = binomial
)

Anova(model)

```

# Signal Detection
We find evidence that identifying that postconditions are incorrect requires 
more cognitive work than identifying that they are correct, and this likely 
drives our observed effects; (1) acceptance of incorrect postconditions varied 
by function (Table II), while a uniform bias would result in similar rates; 
(2) it took longer to reject an incorrect postcondition than accept it, an 
asymmetry which did not exist for correct postconditions; (3) think-aloud 
participants frequently confirmed initial judgements of incorrectness with 
negative examples (18/29 cases) (Section VI-D). With yes/no responses, signal 
detection cannot separate a response bias from asymmetric difficulty, since an 
undetected error looks just like biased acceptance. However, we did fit a signal 
detection model predicting participant response from postcondition correctness. 
Participants did distinguish correct from incorrect postconditions (sensitivity 
d’ = 0.70, p < 0.001), and when unsure they leaned toward calling a 
postcondition correct (criterion c = −0.37, p < 0.001). The three observations 
above indicate that this lean is at least partially due to a difference in 
cognitive difficulty. 
```{r}
lt <- lt |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cond = ifelse(Postcondition_Correct == 1, 0.5, -0.5)   
  )

signal_detection <- glmer(Response_Chosen ~ cond + (1 + cond | Pid) + (1 | Function_Seen),
               data = lt, family = binomial(link = "probit"))

fe <- fixef(signal_detection)
c(d_prime = unname(fe["cond"]), criterion_c = unname(-fe["(Intercept)"]))
```

# Exploratory Docstring Characteristics Analysis 

We fit a generalized linear mixed effects model with participant accuracy as 
the dependent variable, postcondition correctness, scaled docstring word 
count, and their interaction as fixed effects, and individual variability 
and postcondition stimulus 
as random effects. Interestingly, while we did not find a significant 
main effect of docstring length,
there was a significant interaction between docstring word 
count and postcondition correctness ($p < 0.001$, OR = 0.40). At mean 
docstring length, participants had 3.38 times the odds of accurately 
identifying correct postconditions versus incorrect ones. However, this 
gap became smaller with each SD increase in docstring length.
```{r}
model <- glmer(
  Participant_Correct ~ scale(Docstring_Words) * Postcondition_Correct + 
    (1 | Pid) + (1 | Postcondition_Seen),
  family = binomial,
  data = lt,
)

summary(model)

Anova(model)

# Get odds ratios from fixed effects
exp(fixef(model))
```
